title: Breaking And Entering: Pulling Back The Curtain On YEARN IV
summary: One half of the duo behind Triple R’s Album of the Week in May of 2025, Kuya Neil, dropped into the studio on the release week of his and Teether’s collaborative album, YEARN IV. Kuya Neil talks about the behind the scenes of writing the album and its contrast in recording from the duo’s two previously released mixtapes. While the two performing producers have always drawn influence from genres like electronica and metal, Kuya Neil talks about how this time they went down to the Mornington Peninsula to intentionally slow down and refine their sound.
transcript:
Kuya Neil joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios in the release week of YEARN IV, his album with Teether. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 8 May 2025. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: Lauren and I have both been loving the chance to dive deeper into the record after playing all the singles, and really enjoying the fusion of hip-hop, electronic, metal, punk and club music styles. We were talking a little before the break about your history as a producer, and the evolution through all these local, hyper-specific sounds as well as some really international influences. The album is musically expansive, and thematically it looks at alienation, internet-era nostalgia and the search for meaning: some big questions that you and Teether are exploring. But the way it was made is fascinating too. You'd made two mixtapes, GLYPH and STRESSOR, after an initial EP, but for this one you rented a place on the Mornington Peninsula and just dug in. Is that right?

Neil: Yeah. We were in a house for like a week in Rye, on the Mornington Peninsula, where all we did was make music every day, go to the beach, cook food.

Lauren: You've talked about it being like you were teenagers, jamming in your bedrooms.

Neil: Yeah, like their parents were away or something. It was really nice.

Lauren: Because you're from down that way, aren't you?

Neil: Yeah, I'm from Hastings. I don't know if people know where Hastings is, but it's a little bit further down from Frankston, if anyone knows where Frankston is. So it was cool to go back. It was very scenic, a slower pace. I think that's what we really needed at that time, because the year before we had released STRESSOR, and we were just playing shows all the time. So this was a break for us, to get away and focus on music again.

Simon: You make music in all kinds of ways, sharing files over the internet, but perhaps this was a really important way of connecting emotionally and physically.

Neil: Yeah, because we were there together, and we were playing everything together. The process had definitely become more collaborative over the year. During that week we were both playing guitar, playing keyboards. It felt more like a band jamming and making songs together, as opposed to before, when I would be making the beat and Teether would be writing. It was quite a separated process. So this felt very together and very hands-on.

Lauren: Were there unexpected moments that emerged from the jam sessions?

Neil: Yeah, absolutely. A lot of the rock influences came through playing guitar and bass, and having a lot more fun as well, being more silly and playful, because we had that time. We didn't have the pressure we felt a lot the previous year, when we'd have two hours after work or before work, like, 'We have to make a song,' very focused on completing music. So to have this time where we could just play around and let ideas sit and not rush was really, really important.

Simon: Speaking of guitars, you're both fascinated by and experienced in guitar-based music. Teether has talked a lot about his background in metal, and before the break we played a track from Cocteau Twins, a band that I think was pretty important for you. Is that right?

Neil: Yeah, for sure. I've been listening to a lot of Cocteau Twins recently. I really love the guitar tone, and I try to emulate that a bit in the live show.

Simon: And metal? Was that big for you as a kid?

Neil: It was. My cousin Rex from the Philippines taught me the guitar when I was younger, and he was a huge metalhead, and nu metal was really big at the time, like Linkin Park and Papa Roach, bands like that. Playing metal songs as a teenager was the way I got better at the instrument. I wasn't only into that music; I liked a lot of other stuff. But that was probably the most fun to play at home.

Lauren: It's highly technical.

Neil: Yeah, absolutely. It's the most nerdy kind, where musicianship is super important. In a lot of other genres I liked, like punk bands, it wasn't very fashionable to be good at an instrument. It was cool to not know how to play, whereas in metal and stuff, it was all about chops.

Lauren: I read that you and Teether bonded over a shared love of Metallica. Is that right?

Neil: Yeah, we both love Metallica. Teether's probably a bigger Metallica fan than me, but we both listened to a lot of that growing up, and I had all the Metallica DVDs: burnt ones from the Philippines, bootlegs and stuff.

Simon: Talking about nostalgia and your upbringing, something else you've both cited is the importance of early internet culture to this record, and to the project more generally. You've talked about being raised by the internet, and trying to explore that soundscape musically. What does the early internet mean to you, and how does it sound?

Neil: I think lower-quality MP3s, that pre-streaming sort of sound, using software like LimeWire or Kazaa, even early Napster; my sister showed me that stuff early on. It's the process of digging for stuff online at a time when it was a lot more free, the wild, wild west internet.

Simon: The promise of the early internet.

Neil: Yeah, absolutely. It was quite utopian anyway. People could customise their own pages; people had a sense of not only anonymity but autonomy over what they were presenting. There was a lot more of that.

Lauren: Are we talking MySpace pages?

Neil: Yeah, absolutely. Even before MySpace, people would make their own websites. Learning how to code was kind of a thing young people were doing, experimenting with it as a creative thing. Obviously now it's a lot different, but I miss that era a lot.

Simon: Creating your own little universe, too, and identity really forms a core part of this new album as well. Bridging past and present, the record brings together, as I mentioned earlier, hyper-local and global influences. What elements of the Naarm/Melbourne music community and its sound are you including?

Neil: I think so many. For Teether, it would be a lot of the underground rap stuff, particularly what's coming out of the southeast: artists like Chef Chung, and producers like Hawkrada, who are making more lo-fi, abstract hip-hop. And for myself, it would definitely be the club scene. The DJs who are playing at Miscellania and places like that: people playing jungle, people playing ballroom, vogue music, Jersey club, all electronic dance music.

Lauren: The album features a bunch of collaborators too, like Nerdie from 1300, Alice Skye and Stoneset. Can you tell us about their involvement?

Neil: Yeah. Stoneset actually came to the recording session and hung out with us for a few days, and we were sharing songs we were working on, and then the 'DIAL UP' beat: immediately when I heard that, I was like, 'Oh, this is amazing.' So I jumped on it quickly and added a couple of flourishes, and Teether was in the bathroom or something, and when he walked out, we'd already finished the song. So he was like, 'Oh, let's record this.' It was one of those really immediate things where we just fell in love with the sound, and Stoneset's such an incredible producer.

With Alice it was a bit different. We made the song during the writing trip, but the whole time I kept thinking of Natalie Imbruglia's 'Torn' music video. That kept playing in my mind when I was making the track, and I was like, 'Oh, this feels like Australiana,' like watching videos on Rage or something.

Lauren: Was that a big ritual for you growing up?

Neil: Yeah, absolutely. Rage was a big part. That's how I would get put on to a lot of stuff, through music videos. So Alice just felt like the perfect person for that. We were already friends, and we reached out to her, and she was into the track, and we went to her place and recorded it. And who's the other person?

Lauren: Nerdie, from 1300.

Neil: Yeah, that was the first time we ever hung out. We just got some lunch together, and he started playing the guitar. He was just mucking around; he wasn't really playing anything seriously, but I was recording everything. Then I used the guitar parts he made, and produced a track with that. He probably doesn't even really remember it. I've spoken to him about it, and he's like, 'What song is that?' So I don't think it even really registered in his mind, but I really liked it.

Simon: He was deep in the flow state.

Neil: Yeah, probably.

Simon: Speaking of flow, there's a real ebb and flow to the energy of the record. You've released a couple of mixtapes, but this is officially your debut full-length, and you've talked about it being a cohesive narrative and musical statement. Can you tell us about the sequencing of the album, and the story it's telling?

Neil: With the sequencing, honestly, I have to give that to Ben O'Connor from Chapter Music. He's really good at sequencing records. He loves to do it, and I trusted him with that. I had a rough sequence that was maybe more about the order in which things were made, but that doesn't always make sense for listeners.

I feel like we usually start our records with more of a driving, mission-statement kind of song that's quite heavy, and then we just try to throw the listener around. So you'll probably notice there are a lot of shifts in mood. It doesn't really ride a certain feeling consistently. It kind of just jumps around, and I think that just reflects how we consume stuff now.

Everything is pretty jarring. You can be on your phone, scrolling through some of the most intense things ever, and then the stupidest things right straight after.

Lauren: Neil, what are some of the core ideas that you and Teether were keen to communicate on the new record?

Neil: I think we really just wanted to create something that's honest and represents where we're from and where we grew up: an honest representation of that, the reality of it, and how that kind of isolation, or even boredom, is what creates the imagination for music.

Especially being geographically so far away from a lot of the stuff that we're inspired by, I think you can feel quite placeless being here. So that's what we wanted to speak on: the experience of growing up in this country, and the things that are hard about that, but also the things that feed your imagination and make it really special.

Simon: The record is out on Chapter Music, and it's one of the final releases on Chapter in its current form. Can you tell us about your relationship with the label, and how you first connected?

Neil: It was actually through Triple R, I feel like. Paul Gorrie played some of our tracks from God of Surprises, which was our first ever release, through X Amount Records. Shout out to them. And then Chapter contacted us directly. We didn't really have a relationship before that, so it was like meeting for the very first time and then working together for the very first time. But they've been really amazing, honestly. They've been super helpful. They give us so much freedom to express what we want to express, but also a lot of good advice, and they've kind of helped us to take it more seriously.

We definitely come from a bit of a culture of not wanting to take things super seriously, not wanting to have ambition or be career-focused. There's maybe a bit of shame around that. But they made that seem possible without having to compromise on the music. So they've just been amazing. Really friendly, helpful.

They're big fans, and they've been doing it for so long as well. So I feel like they're just good people to have around, because they're in for the long haul, you know?

Simon: There's such a strong alignment between what you're all doing: creating communities, celebrating the artistry of others, really uplifting. There's going to be a celebration of that legacy at Day Tripper. And it's been a big year for you live as well. I think the last time you were on Triple R might have been with Samira on The Score, ahead of Golden Plains. Is that right?

Neil: Yeah, that's right. We had one show at the Gasometer.

Simon: And the Golden Plains set.

Neil: Yeah, that was amazing. It was such a perfect week for us. I hadn't seen Teether, obviously, since he'd moved.

Lauren: The real reunion.

Neil: Yeah, reunion. But it felt like nothing had changed. I picked him up when he was in Footscray. It felt like he'd just gone to Sydney or something, or just gone down the road, you know? It didn't feel weird at all. And that week was just full of seeing friends, playing shows. It was amazing.

Simon: We've lined up 'WAY OUT' to conclude the conversation. What can you tell us about it?

Neil: Oh, 'WAY OUT'. I think this one does capture the feeling of the trip. It's a kind of underwater feeling. We spent a lot of time at the beach, just staring at the ocean, you know, single teardrop, getting sentimental. So this is definitely capturing that.

I think it's a good middle point of the record. It has a lot of footwork and dance music elements, but also a more nostalgic, gentle synth-y sort of line, and it feels kind of organic too. So I think it captures both sides.
aliases: Pulling Back The Curtain On YEARN IV
